title: Śleszyński–Pringsheim theorem
source_statement_excerpt: It states that if $n$ is a positive integer and $(a_{n})$ , $(b_{n})$ are sequences of real numbers such that $|b_{n}|\geq |a_{n}|+1$ for all $n$ , then
statement: For every positive integer $n$, $a_n,b_n\in\mathbb R$ and $|b_n|\ge |a_n|+1$. $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ are sequences of real numbers. The continued fraction $\cfrac{a_1}{b_1+\cfrac{a_2}{b_2+\cfrac{a_3}{b_3+\ddots}}}$ converges absolutely to a value $x$ satisfying $|x|\le 1$.

title: Abel–Ruffini theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the Abel–Ruffini theorem (also known as Abel's impossibility theorem) states that there is no solution in radicals to general polynomial equations of degree five or higher with arbitrary coefficients. Here, general means that the coefficients of the equation are viewed and manipulated as indeterminates.
statement: Consider a general polynomial equation of degree at least five whose coefficients are treated as independent indeterminates. There is no formula expressing its roots in terms of the coefficients using only arithmetic operations and extraction of radicals.
hypotheses: Consider a general polynomial equation of degree at least five whose coefficients are treated as independent indeterminates.
conclusions: There is no formula expressing its roots in terms of the coefficients using only arithmetic operations and extraction of radicals.
editorial_note: Uses the main general-polynomial claim; does not conflate it with the separately mentioned existence of individual unsolvable equations.

title: Adiabatic connection fluctuation dissipation theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In density functional theory (DFT) the adiabatic-connection fluctuation-dissipation theorem (ACFD) is an exact formula for the Kohn–Sham correlation energy. A connection between noninteracting electrons and interacting electrons (the adiabatic connection (AC)) is combined with the random density fluctuations of molecular or solid systems (fluctuation-dissipation (FD)). It is used as a tool in theoretical chemistry and quantum chemistry to approximate the electronic energy.

title: Annulus theorem
source_statement_excerpt: If S and T are topological spheres in Euclidean space, with S contained in T, then it is not true in general that the region between them is an annulus, because of the existence of wild spheres in dimension at least 3. So the annulus theorem has to be stated to exclude these examples, by adding some condition to ensure that S and T are well behaved. There are several ways to do this.
statement: Let $B$ be the closed unit ball in $\mathbb R^n$ and let $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be a homeomorphism such that $h(B)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(B)$. $B\setminus h(\operatorname{int}B)$ is homeomorphic to $S^{n-1}\times[0,1]$.
hypotheses: Let $B$ be the closed unit ball in $\mathbb R^n$ and let $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be a homeomorphism such that $h(B)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(B)$.
conclusions: $B\setminus h(\operatorname{int}B)$ is homeomorphic to $S^{n-1}\times[0,1]$.
editorial_note: Selects the explicit equivalent homeomorphism formulation rather than the informal wild-spheres discussion.

title: Argument principle
source_statement_excerpt: If f is a meromorphic function inside and on some closed contour C, and f has no zeros or poles on C, then
statement: Let $C$ be a simple closed counterclockwise contour, and let $f$ be meromorphic on and inside $C$, with no zero or pole on $C$. $\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=Z-P$, where $Z$ counts zeros within $C$ with multiplicity and $P$ counts poles with order.
hypotheses: Let $C$ be a simple closed counterclockwise contour, and let $f$ be meromorphic on and inside $C$, with no zero or pole on $C$.
conclusions: $\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=Z-P$, where $Z$ counts zeros within $C$ with multiplicity and $P$ counts poles with order.

title: Artin's theorem on induced characters
source_statement_excerpt: Let $G$ be a finite group and $X$ any family of subgroups.
statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $\mathcal X$ a family of subgroups of $G$. The following are equivalent: (i) $G=\bigcup_{g\in G,H\in\mathcal X}g^{-1}Hg$; (ii) for every character $\chi$ of $G$ there are characters $\chi_H$ of $H$ for $H\in\mathcal X$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $n\chi=\sum_{H\in\mathcal X}\operatorname{Ind}_{H}^{G}(\chi_H)$.

conclusions: The following are equivalent: (i) $G=\bigcup_{g\in G,H\in\mathcal X}g^{-1}Hg$; (ii) for every character $\chi$ of $G$ there are characters $\chi_H$ of $H$ for $H\in\mathcal X$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $n\chi=\sum_{H\in\mathcal X}\operatorname{Ind}_{H}^{G}(\chi_H)$.

title: Atkinson's theorem

title: Bézout's identity
source_statement_excerpt: Bézout's identity—Let a and b be integers with greatest common divisor d. Then there exist integers x and y such that ax + by = d. Moreover, the integers of the form az + bt are exactly the multiples of d.
statement: Let $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ and $d=\gcd(a,b)$, with $\gcd(0,0)=0$. There exist $x,y\in\mathbb Z$ such that $ax+by=d$. The set $\{az+bt:z,t\in\mathbb Z\}$ is precisely $d\mathbb Z$.
hypotheses: Let $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ and $d=\gcd(a,b)$, with $\gcd(0,0)=0$.
conclusions: There exist $x,y\in\mathbb Z$ such that $ax+by=d$.

title: Baker's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In transcendental number theory, a mathematical discipline, Baker's theorem gives a lower bound for the absolute value of linear combinations of logarithms of algebraic numbers. Nearly fifteen years earlier, Alexander Gelfond had considered the problem with only integer coefficients to be of "extraordinarily great significance". The result, proved by Alan Baker (1966, 1967a, 1967b), subsumed many earlier results in transcendental number theory. Baker used this to prove the transcendence of many numbers, to derive effective bounds for the solutions of some Diophantine equations, and to solve the class number problem of finding all imaginary quadratic fields with class number 1.

title: Barbier's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In geometry, Barbier's theorem states that every curve of constant width has perimeter π times its width, regardless of its precise shape. This theorem was first published by Joseph-Émile Barbier in 1860.
statement: Let $\gamma$ be a plane curve of constant width $w$. The perimeter of $\gamma$ is $\pi w$.
hypotheses: Let $\gamma$ be a plane curve of constant width $w$.

title: Beck–Fiala theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the Beck–Fiala theorem is a major theorem in discrepancy theory due to József Beck and Tibor Fiala. Discrepancy is concerned with coloring elements of a ground set such that each set in a certain set system is as balanced as possible, i.e., has approximately the same number of elements of each color. The Beck–Fiala theorem is concerned with the case where each element doesn't appear many times across all sets. The theorem guarantees that if each element appears at most t times, then the elements can be colored so that the imbalance is at most 2t − 1. Beck and Fiala conjectured that the imbalance can be even bounded by $O({\sqrt {t}})$ .
statement: Let $S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[n]$ be a finite set system and let $t$ be a positive integer such that each $i\in[n]$ belongs to at most $t$ of these sets. There is a coloring $x:[n]\to\{-1,+1\}$ such that for all $1\le j\le m$, $\left|\sum_{i\in S_j}x(i)\right|\le 2t-1$.
hypotheses: Let $S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[n]$ be a finite set system and let $t$ be a positive integer such that each $i\in[n]$ belongs to at most $t$ of these sets.
conclusions: There is a coloring $x:[n]\to\{-1,+1\}$ such that for all $1\le j\le m$, $\left|\sum_{i\in S_j}x(i)\right|\le 2t-1$.
editorial_note: Restores the quantified coloring and the exact $2t-1$ bound from the statement section; excludes the conjectured stronger bound.

title: Bendixson–Dulac theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the Bendixson–Dulac theorem is a theorem in dynamical systems that exclude the existence of periodic orbits of two-dimensional flows. Here a flow can be visualized as the surface of a pond. If you drop a leaf into a pond, it will drift according to the currents in the water, and a periodic orbit is when the leaf returns to the same place. Roughly speaking, the theorem states that if it is possible to distort the field of currents by stretching and compressing the pond like a rubber sheet, in such a way that the flow is either always expanding or always contracting, then there is no periodic orbit.
statement: Consider the planar autonomous system $\dot x=f(x,y)$, $\dot y=g(x,y)$ on a simply connected plane region, and suppose there exists a $C^1$ Dulac function $\varphi(x,y)$ such that $\partial_x(\varphi f)+\partial_y(\varphi g)$ has a constant nonzero sign almost everywhere in that region. The system has no nonconstant periodic solution lying entirely in the region.
hypotheses: Consider the planar autonomous system $\dot x=f(x,y)$, $\dot y=g(x,y)$ on a simply connected plane region, and suppose there exists a $C^1$ Dulac function $\varphi(x,y)$ such that $\partial_x(\varphi f)+\partial_y(\varphi g)$ has a constant nonzero sign almost everywhere in that region.
conclusions: The system has no nonconstant periodic solution lying entirely in the region.
editorial_note: Uses the formal Dulac criterion, not the informal flow analogy.

title: Binomial theorem
source_statement_excerpt: This formula is also referred to as the binomial formula or the binomial identity. Using summation notation, it can be written more concisely as
statement: Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $x,y$ be commuting elements of a commutative ring. $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k$, where $\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$.

conclusions: $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k$, where $\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$.

title: Bloch's theorem

The theorem is named after the Swiss physicist Felix Bloch, who discovered the theorem in 1929. Mathematically, they are written

title: Bohr–Van Leeuwen theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The Bohr–Van Leeuwen theorem states that when statistical mechanics and classical mechanics are applied consistently, the thermal average of the magnetization is always zero. This makes magnetism in solids solely a quantum mechanical effect and means that classical physics cannot account for paramagnetism, diamagnetism and ferromagnetism. The inability of classical physics to explain triboelectricity also stems from the Bohr–Van Leeuwen theorem.
statement: Consider a classical statistical-mechanical treatment of a system in thermal equilibrium, using classical mechanics and statistical mechanics consistently. The thermal average of the magnetization is zero.
hypotheses: Consider a classical statistical-mechanical treatment of a system in thermal equilibrium, using classical mechanics and statistical mechanics consistently.
conclusions: The thermal average of the magnetization is zero.

title: Burnside's lemma
source_statement_excerpt: Burnside's lemma, sometimes also called Burnside's counting theorem, the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma, or the orbit-counting theorem, is a result in group theory that is often useful in taking account of symmetry when counting mathematical objects. It was discovered by Augustin Louis Cauchy and Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, and became well known after William Burnside quoted it. The result enumerates orbits of a symmetry group acting on some objects: that is, it counts distinct objects, considering objects symmetric to each other as the same; or counting distinct objects up to a symmetry equivalence relation; or counting only objects in canonical form. For example, in describing possible organic compounds of certain type, one considers them up to spatial rotation symmetry: different rotated drawings of a given molecule are chemically identical (whereas a mirror reflection might give a different compound).
statement: Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $X$, and let $X^g=\{x\in X:g\cdot x=x\}$. The number of $G$-orbits is $|X/G|=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|X^g|$.
hypotheses: Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $X$, and let $X^g=\{x\in X:g\cdot x=x\}$.
conclusions: The number of $G$-orbits is $|X/G|=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|X^g|$.
editorial_note: Uses the finite-set orbit-counting formula in the statement section.

title: Byers–Yang theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In quantum mechanics, the Byers–Yang theorem states that all physical properties of a doubly connected system (an annulus) enclosing a magnetic flux $\Phi $ through the opening are periodic in the flux with period $\Phi _{0}=hc/e$ (the magnetic flux quantum). The theorem was first stated and proven by Nina Byers and Chen-Ning Yang (1961), and further developed by Felix Bloch (1970).
statement: Consider a doubly connected quantum system enclosing magnetic flux $\Phi$. Every physical property is periodic in $\Phi$ with flux period $\Phi_0=hc/e$.
hypotheses: Consider a doubly connected quantum system enclosing magnetic flux $\Phi$.
conclusions: Every physical property is periodic in $\Phi$ with flux period $\Phi_0=hc/e$.

title: Carathéodory's extension theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $\Sigma _{0}$ be an algebra of subsets of a set $X.$ Consider a set function $\mu _{0}:\Sigma _{0}\to [0,\infty ]$ that is sigma additive, meaning that $\mu _{0}\left(\bigcup _{n=1}^{\infty }A_{n}\right)=\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\mu _{0}(A_{n})$ for any disjoint family $\{A_{n}:n\in \mathbb {N} \}$ of elements of $\Sigma _{0}$ such that $\cup _{n=1}^{\infty }A_{n}\in \Sigma _{0}.$ (Functions $\mu _{0}$ obeying these two properties are known as pre-measures.) Then, $\mu _{0}$ extends to a measure defined on the $\sigma $ -algebra $\Sigma $ generated by $\Sigma _{0}$ ; that is, there exists a measure $\mu :\Sigma \to [0,\infty ]$ such that its restriction to $\Sigma _{0}$ coincides with $\mu _{0}.$
statement: Let $\Sigma_0$ be an algebra of subsets of a set $X$ and let $\mu_0:\Sigma_0\to[0,\infty]$ be a premeasure, meaning it is countably additive on pairwise disjoint families whose union lies in $\Sigma_0$. There exists a measure $\mu:\sigma(\Sigma_0)\to[0,\infty]$ such that $\mu|_{\Sigma_0}=\mu_0$.
hypotheses: Let $\Sigma_0$ be an algebra of subsets of a set $X$ and let $\mu_0:\Sigma_0\to[0,\infty]$ be a premeasure, meaning it is countably additive on pairwise disjoint families whose union lies in $\Sigma_0$.
conclusions: There exists a measure $\mu:\sigma(\Sigma_0)\to[0,\infty]$ such that $\mu|_{\Sigma_0}=\mu_0$.
editorial_note: States the existence part from the introductory statement; no unqualified uniqueness assertion.

title: Carleman's inequality

statement: Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers. $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_1a_2\cdots a_n)^{1/n}\le e\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n$. The constant $e$ is optimal; if some $a_n>0$, the inequality is strict.

conclusions: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_1a_2\cdots a_n)^{1/n}\le e\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n$.
